input.topic: Hyperthyroidism: Ligand-Receptor Cross-Reactivity Of ß-Hcg And TSH

expected.question_text: A 23-year-old man with recently diagnosed testicular choriocarcinoma is referred to an endocrinologist because he has been experiencing sweating, weight loss, diarrhea, and a sensation that his heart is racing. He is currently on bleomycin for treatment of his cancer. The most likely pathophysiologic mechanism of the symptoms is the
expected.explanation_header: The correct answer is α subunit cross-reactivity between human chorionic gonadotropin and thyroid-stimulating hormone.
expected.explanation_footer:
This patient with recently diagnosed testicular choriocarcinoma likely has paraneoplastic hyperthyroidism , supported by his presentation of sweating, weight loss, diarrhea, and heart palpitations (eg, sensation that his heart is racing). Choriocarcinoma secretes large amounts of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) . The β subunit of hCG is similar to that of luteinizing hormone (LH), explaining its gonadotropic effect. However, the α subunit of hCG is similar to that of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) , causing cross-reactivity . Consequently, patients can have symptoms of paraneoplastic hyperthyroidism. TSH, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), and LH are glycoproteins consisting of 2 subunits, α and β. The α subunits of TSH, FSH, and LH are identical and are synthesized from the same mRNA. The β subunits for each hormone are different and have their own biologic specificity. However, compared to other hormones, the β subunits contain some homology. The hCG is also structurally related to the TSH-FSH-LH hormone family. Patients with nonseminomatous testicular cancers can have markedly elevated levels of hCG. Due to hormone subunit homology, there is some cross-reactivity at certain hormone receptors . In 1 study, 3.5% of nonseminomatous germ cell tumor cases revealed clinical hyperthyroidism due to hCG and TSH cross-reactivity. Some testicular cancer patients can also exhibit gynecomastia through hCG and LH homology.
